chapters.title: Love
chapters.hook: 1 unread text makes you build a whole future before you even tap it.
chapters.counterintuition: You may read the fading rush as proof the love went bad. In fact, the brain may have learned the reward so well that surprise no longer fires.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next task handoff, move the app or thread you chase for a rush behind one extra tap, then rehearse opening the useful next task once.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Dopamine makes the possible feel urgent, not the possessed feel complete; when the rush fades, shift from chasing proof to building present trust.

breakdown.fastRead: Your thumb hovers over an unread text, and your mind has already spent the weekend. You picture the date, the apartment, the future laugh at the sink. Then the real reply arrives: warm, normal, human. The glow dips, and you wonder what went wrong. Dopamine is the brain chemical that tags possible rewards. It loves the gap between maybe and mine. Wanting paints with future light. The rush is a scout, not a home. When love becomes close, the task changes. Stop asking newness to prove truth. Build trust, touch, and shared days.
breakdown.deepRead:
A cue pulls harder when it still carries news. Reward prediction error means the brain sees a gap between what it forecast and what arrived. If the result is better than expected, the signal jumps. If the result is old news, the signal calms down. So a message bubble can feel larger than the date itself.

At the University of Fribourg, Wolfram Schultz worked with macaque monkeys while cues predicted food. The later 1997 Science frame with Peter Dayan and P. Read Montague read dopamine as an update signal for future rewards. Once the monkey learned the cue, the food did not have to surprise the cell. The cue did the work. Your dating life has its own cues: the three dots, the coat on the chair, the possible weekend. The imagined reward spreads wider than the real hour can hold.

Wanting and liking also split. Wanting is the push toward a thing. Liking is the pleasure once it is here. You can chase the text with force and still feel only a small warmth when it arrives. Nothing false has been exposed. The chase used more future than the moment could repay. Wanting asks, what might happen? Liking asks, how does this feel now? Confuse those two, and you blame a steady partner for no longer acting like a surprise machine.
breakdown.fullRead:
In a lab near London in 1957, Katharine Montagu found dopamine in human brain tissue at Runwell Hospital. That detail matters because the story starts with a real chemical, not a dating slogan. At first, dopamine looked like a step on the way to other brain chemicals. Later work gave it a larger role: it helps mark what might be gained next.

A cup in your hand and a trail marker across the road ask different things of the brain. John Douglas Pettigrew's path from Wagga Wagga to the University of Queensland keeps the spatial frame concrete. The source names two spatial worlds: peripersonal present and extrapersonal future. Peripersonal present is the cup in your hand, the partner on the couch, the kiss that is happening now. Extrapersonal future is across the room, down the road, or years ahead. What cannot be reached must be imagined.

A new lover lives, for a while, across that road. If the reward is not here yet, you have to picture it, plan for it, and move toward it. That is why a new love can swell so fast. One reply becomes a house, a trip, a child, a life where your old hurts stop hurting. The person is real, but the glowing future is partly your own build.

Three reward components keep the story straight: wanting, liking, and learning. Wanting pulls you forward. Liking is the taste of the reward now. Learning updates the map after the world answers back. You may want the first date more than you like the second month. You may learn that the real person is kinder, messier, quieter, or less free than the person your mind previewed.

The second month can feel calmer without being worse. The first rush can get you close enough to notice someone. After that, love has to change jobs. Trust is made in present time. Touch is made in present time. Shared chores, honest calls, and familiar meals are made in present time. Familiar joy can be real without being new.

A blue typing bubble can spend the evening you meant to use. You chase the next reply, then miss the actual chance to say the kind thing while it still counts. The window closes. The person goes to sleep hurt, or the form due before midnight sits untouched. The future in your head spent the present in your hands.

A partner who lies, harms you, or keeps vanishing is not asking for a chemistry lesson. Do not call the fading rush maturity and stay. Dopamine can explain why the first pull was bright. It cannot make neglect into attachment. In that case, the present is giving you evidence.

At the next cue, ask which system you are feeding. If you are feeding wanting, you will keep searching for the next sign. If you are feeding liking and trust, you will notice the person in reach. The future can invite you. It cannot hold you.

examples.title: Cue Light Yield
examples.scenario: The food cup is still, but the cue light has both lab coders leaning over the trace. During a reward-coding pass with macaque monkeys in Wolfram Schultz's University of Fribourg lab, Piper says, "The pleasure is the food." Marlene taps the earlier spike. "The news is the cue." Piper follows the line again, then nods. "I was reading the bite. The cell is reading the promise."
examples.whatToDo: Piper changes the coding note from food pleasure to cue prediction. She lets Marlene's read stand because the trace shows surprise moving earlier.
examples.whyItMatters: The concession makes the mechanism visible. Dopamine is tracking useful news about a coming reward, not just cheering after the reward lands.

examples.title: Runwell Label Repair
examples.scenario: The tray is already marked "precursor" when Quentin sees the problem. He had filed Katharine Montagu's Runwell Hospital finding that way because dopamine looked like a step toward other chemicals. The 1957 brain tissue result is in front of him, and the word on the tray now feels too small. He crosses it out and writes, "measure this on its own."
examples.whatToDo: Quentin corrects his own label before the old shortcut spreads. He keeps the Runwell result visible as a discovery, not a footnote to another chemical.
examples.whyItMatters: The repair protects the history. Dopamine entered the story as a measured brain chemical before anyone sold it as a pop pleasure word.

examples.title: Cue Column Memo
examples.scenario: "Do not score the food as the whole reward," Bennett writes at the top of the lab memo. In Wolfram Schultz's work with macaque monkeys, the cue trace is forcing a choice: keep the old pleasure note or update the next coding pass. Bennett's memo says the cell is marking a future reward, so the cue column moves left of the food column.
examples.whatToDo: Bennett rewrites the memo around the cue. He makes the next lab pass mark when prediction starts, not only when food arrives.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo makes anticipation visible on paper. A cue can carry the force of the future before the reward itself is in hand.

examples.title: Cup And Ridge
examples.scenario: The close cup and the distant ridge ask for opposite kinds of attention. In a University of Queensland field lesson, Mathieu keeps his hand around coffee near the Wagga Wagga trail map. Colby traces the ridge line before stepping off. John Douglas Pettigrew's near-and-far space work gives the scene its names. The cup is within reach; the ridge has to be planned.
examples.whatToDo: Colby keeps the far object in view long enough to plan a route. Mathieu handles the near comfort well but loses the path once the map is shut.
examples.whyItMatters: Dopamine belongs to what is not yet in reach. The contrast shows why desire needs maps, not just feelings about what is already in hand.

examples.title: Joy Meter Correction
examples.scenario: The senior tutor is home sick, and Deborah gets the chalk, the model brain, and five minutes with the trainee who keeps calling dopamine a pleasure button. In a Runwell Hospital teaching room, she says, "Katharine Montagu found the chemical. She did not find a joy meter." The trainee frowns. Deborah adds, "A signal can pull you forward without proving you will enjoy the arrival."
examples.whatToDo: Deborah replaces the pleasure-button phrase with wanting versus liking. She makes the trainee say which part belongs to pursuit and which belongs to enjoyment.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe stops a common romance mistake. A strong chase does not prove deep pleasure, and a calmer present does not prove love has failed.

examples.title: Two Squares Lesson
examples.scenario: John Douglas Pettigrew shades the far square instead of the cup while the University of Queensland class is still arguing about which one counts as space. A learner points to Wagga Wagga on the map and then to the cup. Pettigrew keeps the confusion on the board: the cup can be touched now; the town has to be imagined, mapped, and pursued.
examples.whatToDo: Pettigrew leaves both squares visible and makes the learner place each object by reach. The class has to name what the hand can touch and what planning must reach.
examples.whyItMatters: The school case turns a brain map into daily life. What is beyond reach pulls on imagination because action must cross time and distance first.

questions.prompt: A podcast host says dopamine began as a catchy pleasure slogan, then labs searched for proof. Which correction fits the history?
choices: The slogan came first, and later labs gave the pleasure idea a chemical name.
The discovery was mainly a romance metaphor, and lab work made it memorable.
The chemical was identified in brain tissue before pleasure labels attached to it.
questions.explanation: Montagu's Runwell work places dopamine in lab biochemistry first. The pleasure shortcut came later and can hide that chemical history.

questions.prompt: A lab log shows macaque neurons firing when a cue predicts food, then quieting when food is expected. Which reading fits the data?
choices: Dopamine is best read as a signal that rises during the food itself.
Dopamine is best read as proof that learned food keeps the same charge.
Dopamine is best read as an update signal tied to future rewards.
questions.explanation: The cue shift is the key. Once food is expected, dopamine marks the prediction update rather than simple pleasure at the bite.

questions.prompt: A cafe reward once felt exciting, but the same free drink now feels routine. Which inference about prediction error is strongest?
choices: The surprise has shrunk, so the update signal has less to mark.
The predictable drink should create the largest dopamine spike each time.
The routine drink proves the reward itself has stopped having value.
questions.explanation: Prediction error depends on a gap between forecast and outcome. A routine reward can still be good while carrying less surprise.

questions.prompt: At a trailhead, a learner touches the water bottle beside her boot and points to a ridge beyond the trees. Which distinction fits?
choices: Both objects belong to one attitude about travel, since each can guide action.
The bottle and ridge differ mainly in mood, since both are outside the body.
The bottle sits in peripersonal present, while the ridge belongs to extrapersonal future.
questions.explanation: Peripersonal present means within reach. Extrapersonal future names what lies outside reach and needs planning across space and time.

questions.prompt: During a grocery checkout line, a reader keeps checking a dating app and feels flat after each match arrives. Which split explains the pattern?
choices: High dopamine means each match should feel more enjoyable once obtained.
Wanting can keep the chase strong while liking stays modest after arrival.
Liking drives the search, while wanting handles the calm after each match.
questions.explanation: Wanting and liking can come apart. The app can energize pursuit without making the obtained match equally satisfying.

questions.prompt: A new partner sends short texts, and each one launches trips, sex, and a shared apartment in your mind. What is the safest read?
choices: The texts prove long-term fit because the imagined future feels detailed.
Uncertainty lets each cue imply many possible rewards before routine tests fit.
Short texts lower dopamine because no real reward has happened yet.
questions.explanation: New romance is potent because one cue can stand for many possible futures. That intensity does not prove compatibility by itself.

questions.prompt: A couple's favorite cafe feels less electric after months of Saturday visits, though the coffee is still good. What changed first?
choices: The surprise faded because the brain now forecasts the pleasant routine.
The cafe lost its value because the old rush no longer appears.
The couple needs a first-week rush to prove the place still matters.
questions.explanation: Familiarity can lower prediction error without lowering quality. The near miss is treating a smaller rush as proof the object got worse.

questions.prompt: During a handoff between tasks, a notification dot appears before the message loads, and you feel pulled to open it. What gives the dot force?
choices: The final message is the only thing that can motivate opening the app.
The cue compresses future possibility into a signal you can act on now.
The dot works only after the reward has been consumed many times.
questions.explanation: A cue can motivate before the reward arrives. The dot gets force by pointing toward a possible future message.

questions.prompt: Two partners miss the first-month rush and wonder if they should keep chasing novelty. Which move fits durable attachment?
choices: Shift attention toward present trust, touch, and shared routine.
Keep the future unresolved so dopamine keeps the bond intense.
Judge the bond by whether each week feels like the first one.
questions.explanation: Long love cannot run on novelty alone. The source points toward present bonds once dopamine's future charge quiets.

reviewCards.front: Why can a cue feel stronger than the reward it predicts?
reviewCards.back: When a cue carries new information about a future reward, dopamine can move toward the cue. Once the reward is expected, the reward itself may carry less surprise.

reviewCards.front: How does reach change the brain's job?
reviewCards.back: Peripersonal present names what your hand can use now. Extrapersonal future names what lies beyond reach and must be imagined, planned for, and pursued.

reviewCards.front: Why can wanting outrun liking in early love?
reviewCards.back: Wanting drives pursuit of what may be gained. Liking is the pleasure of what is here. A person can chase a partner or message hard, then feel less pleasure after arrival.

reviewCards.front: Why can familiar pleasure lose the first rush without becoming worse?
reviewCards.back: Familiarity lowers surprise. The cafe, partner, or pleasure may still be good, but the brain no longer reads it as better than expected.

reviewCards.front: What shift does durable attachment need after novelty quiets?
reviewCards.back: It needs a move from future-oriented desire toward present bonds: trust, touch, and shared routine. Long love uses more than the chemistry of pursuit.

reviewCards.front: Why does Montagu's Runwell Hospital finding matter for this idea?
reviewCards.back: It grounds dopamine in a real 1957 brain-tissue discovery before the pleasure-molecule shortcut. The history keeps the idea tied to chemistry, not slogan.

implementationPlan.title: Check the Wanting Gap
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice noticing when the chase is larger than the thing you get. Check the Wanting Gap by naming the cue, the future it promises, and the present contact you can test. The aim is not to kill desire. It is to stop desire from pretending it has already proved satisfaction.

ifThenPlans.context: If a cue makes you build a future before the reward arrives.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the cue starts the movie, then Check the Wanting Gap. Name the cue and wait for the real contact before you treat the future as evidence.

ifThenPlans.context: If a familiar partner or pleasure feels less electric.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old rush is quieter, then Check the Wanting Gap. Look for the lost surprise before you decide the person or pleasure got worse.

ifThenPlans.context: If the waiting felt better than the having.
ifThenPlans.plan: If pursuit beat arrival, then Check the Wanting Gap. Separate wanting from liking before you chase a stronger version.

ifThenPlans.context: If a relationship feels calmer and you want a new spark.
ifThenPlans.plan: If calm reads as failure, then Check the Wanting Gap. Choose one present bond to feed before you shop for novelty.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, stage one task transition once. Put a tempting cue one step away, say the future it promises, then open the present task.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, replace one novelty check with one present-contact act for the same person or task. Compare the week's first half with the second: chase energy versus steadiness.

memorableLines.why: It separates first pursuit from lasting attachment.

memorableLines.text: A cue pulls harder when it still carries news.
memorableLines.why: It gives prediction error a plain image.

memorableLines.text: What cannot be reached must be imagined.
memorableLines.why: It makes far-space desire easy to remember.

chapters.title: Drugs
chapters.hook: I used to think the wiped PET room meant the craving had ended.
chapters.counterintuition: Why does the urge survive after the fun is gone? Dopamine can make cues feel like orders while liking has already thinned.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next unscheduled break, place a short calendar block in your usual break spot and remove one relief cue.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Addiction grows when fast drug surges teach cues to command pursuit; relief can keep calling for the person trying to stop, long after pleasure and choice have thinned.

breakdown.fastRead:
The PET room is wiped down, and the clean room says the story should be over. The person went home. The scan ended. The obvious myth says addiction is pleasure that won too many times. That myth misses the crueler engine.

Drug wanting is a taught chase. A fast surge makes the brain mark the act, the room, the route, and the mood that came before it. Later, the cue can pull before any drug appears.

Wanting can outlive liking. The fix is not scolding desire as weak. You cut one cue in the chain and give control a few more seconds to speak.
breakdown.deepRead:
One press in a lab cage can teach too much. In 1954, James Olds and Peter Milner showed that rats would work to trigger electrical stimulation in reward-related brain regions. There was no sweet fruit at the end. The action itself had become tied to a brain signal worth repeating.

Human drugs make that lesson sharper and more dangerous. Cocaine is not just a story a person tells about a high. Nora Volkow's imaging work tied cocaine effects to dopamine transporter occupancy and reward-pathway activity. A fast chemical change gives the brain a tight time stamp. It links the act with the surge.

The addiction loop has five parts: surge, cue learning, sensitized wanting, control erosion, and relapse risk. Sensitized means the system gets jumpier after repeat use. A cue is a promise with teeth. The doorway, the lighter, the route home, or the bad mood can start the chase before the person has chosen much at all.

The clean split came from Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson. In 1998 Brain Research Reviews, the wanting and liking distinction made addiction easier to see. Dopamine is more about wanting incentives than liking them. That is why a person can chase a drug that gives less joy than it once did. The chase has learned its own path.
breakdown.fullRead:
The cost shows up in a small empty space. Stella deletes one old contact before leaving work, then sits with the blank line where an easy promise used to live. No one claps. No crisis ends. She has simply made the next cue harder to reach, and that tiny subtraction feels like losing a private exit.

That is the price of applying this idea. You give up some relief on purpose. A person who uses a drug for escape is not only chasing fun. Often they are trying to end a bad state fast. Stress, shame, or pain can make relief feel like the most practical thing in the world. The brain learns that shortcut, then starts asking for it early.

This is why compassion has to be exact. Addiction is not a simple preference for intoxication. It is impaired control plus sensitized motivation. The pursuit system has been trained by strong chemical signals, tight timing, and cues that forecast relief. A person may know the costs and still feel pulled by the old chain.

Nora Volkow's cocaine imaging matters here because it gives the moral story a body. The dopamine transporter is not an excuse. It is a place where the story touches tissue. When the drug changes signaling fast, the brain has an easier time crediting the act. The lesson is physical enough to survive shame.

Berridge and Robinson's split also protects you from a false hope. Less pleasure does not mean less risk. Tolerance can dull the high while sensitized wanting keeps the cue bright. The person may say, honestly, that it is not even that good anymore. Then the old street, song, or message thread lights up pursuit.

You have felt a harmless version of this. A buried message sits in a flooded group chat. You mean to answer it, then another alert pulls you. Hours pass, and the relationship cools a little. Addiction is not the same as a missed reply, but the shape is familiar: the cue that flashes first can steal the next action.

The reader's move is smaller than the disease. Cut the Cue Chain means you remove one link before the pull starts. You do not try to win a debate with craving at full volume. You move the old number, skip the old route, ask someone else to hold the spare cash, or leave the risky gap filled with a plan.

The price of protecting wanting is giving up some easy relief. Celine feels it when she walks past the shortcut and takes the longer street home. The longer street costs time. It also buys a few seconds in which the future can speak. That is the trade: less instant escape, more room to stay free.

examples.title: The Cage Click
examples.scenario: Research aide Connor hears the dry click from the film reel in the lab record room before he notices the line in the 1954 log. Reviewing James Olds and Peter Milner's self-stimulation records, he sees the shift: the rat was not working for food or water. The action led to electrical stimulation in reward-related brain regions. One small act in the cage had become its own reason to happen again.
examples.whatToDo: Connor marks the exact finding in the audit: the repeated action was reinforced by direct brain stimulation, not by an ordinary treat outside the animal.
examples.whyItMatters: The lab record makes compulsion less mysterious. A behavior can become self-reinforcing when the reward circuit itself is driven.

examples.title: Stella's Old Contact
examples.scenario: Recovery counselor Stella's thumb stalls above the old contact on her phone in the clinic stairwell after the evening meeting, then curls back. I do not even like that night anymore, she thinks. So why does the name still pull? Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson fit the thought she hates: wanting can stay loud while liking gets thin. The 1998 Brain Research Reviews distinction is not schoolwork now. It is the gap between sending and deleting.
examples.whatToDo: Stella deletes the contact before arguing with the urge. She treats the name as a cue, not as proof that the old pleasure was worth chasing.
examples.whyItMatters: The private scene shows the hard edge. Craving can survive the loss of fun, so the cue has to be handled before it becomes a plan.

examples.title: One Scanner Slot
examples.scenario: One PET slot. Coralie has that much space on the board before the cocaine imaging day fills. Nora Volkow's finding changes what she protects: not another broad mood form, but the timing around dopamine transporter occupancy. If the team misses the fast link between dose and effect, the scan will look like a diary with expensive lights.
examples.whatToDo: Coralie reserves the prep time for timing, transporter measures, and the subject's reported effects instead of spreading attention across loose mood notes.
examples.whyItMatters: The plan keeps the biology visible. Fast chemical change teaches the brain more forcefully when the act and the surge sit close together.

examples.title: Kevin's Alert
examples.scenario: Peer mentor Kevin is typing a sponsor reply outside the Thursday recovery group when a second alert covers the thread. It is the same block where he used to buy, and the map preview hits like weather. He is torn between opening it and risking the pull, or ignoring the phone and missing the one message asking if he is safe. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson's cue work, later laid out in 1998 Brain Research Reviews, feels painfully exact.
examples.whatToDo: Kevin calls the sponsor from the lock screen and leaves the map unopened. He answers the relationship without feeding the cue that is trying to steer him.
examples.whyItMatters: Withdrawal can end while cue power remains. The safer move handles the human need without giving the old signal a fresh path.

examples.title: Before the Scan Window
examples.scenario: There is not much scanner time left in the control room, and PET technologist Celine keeps the cocaine protocol open while William checks the subject sheet. "So we are measuring bad choices?" he asks. "No," Celine says. "Nora Volkow's point is tighter. Dopamine transporter occupancy and reward-pathway activity help explain why the high lands the way it does." William nods. "So the story has tissue in it."
examples.whatToDo: Celine keeps the handoff tied to cocaine, dopamine transporter occupancy, and the timing of reported effects rather than a moral label.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange gives shame less room to masquerade as science. Measurable brain changes do not excuse harm, but they explain why pursuit can feel driven.

examples.title: The Pleasure Gap
examples.scenario: The pleasure score was falling while the cue calls rose. Yann expected the lower high to mean lower risk, so the relapse log should have looked safer by Friday. It did not. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson had warned why in the 1998 Brain Research Reviews split: liking can shrink while wanting keeps the cue bright.
examples.whatToDo: Yann rewrites the risk note around cues, not pleasure ratings. He plans for the old trigger even though the reported high has lost force.
examples.whyItMatters: The reveal blocks a common false hope. A duller drug can still be dangerous when the cue system has learned to chase it.

questions.prompt: A lab archive from 1954 shows rats repeating an action when it triggers stimulation in reward-related brain tissue, with no food in the box. Which claim fits the record?
choices: Modern scanners were the first tools to connect reward with brain activity.
The rats were likely chasing food cues that the archive failed to record.
Direct brain stimulation could reinforce behavior without an ordinary reward.
questions.explanation: Olds and Milner showed that stimulation itself could reinforce behavior. The lesson did not have to wait for scanners or ordinary food rewards.

questions.prompt: A PET report on cocaine shows subjective effects tracking dopamine transporter occupancy and a fast chemical shift. What should the clinician focus on?
choices: The client's craving is separate from dopamine transport and should be read mainly as habit.
The total amount used matters, while onset speed adds little to the learning.
The transporter link and rapid onset help the brain pair use with reward.
questions.explanation: Cocaine effects connect to dopamine transporters, and timing matters. A rapid shift helps the brain connect the act with reward.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "If the drug stops feeling good, the addiction should fade." Which reply fits the wanting and liking split?
choices: Less pleasure means the cue has lost most of its pull for that person.
Wanting can keep rising even when the high feels thinner.
Pleasure is the safest guide to how strong craving will be.
questions.explanation: The split says dopamine is more tied to wanting than liking. The high can thin while pursuit remains strong.

questions.prompt: A recovery log shows no acute withdrawal symptoms for months, then a familiar street starts a strong craving. Which reading fits incentive sensitization?
choices: The old cue can still wake pursuit after withdrawal has passed.
The withdrawal timeline was measured poorly, so the craving belongs to the body only.
The street matters mainly as a memory, not as a trigger for pursuit.
questions.explanation: Cue salience can last after physical withdrawal fades. The old street can reactivate pursuit before any drug is taken.

questions.prompt: A public health presenter says opioids, alcohol, and stimulants must each use unrelated reward systems. What correction fits the dopamine frame?
choices: Different drug classes can only be compared after their social harms match.
Different mechanisms can still meet in reward-pathway dopamine activity.
Drug differences matter so much that shared motivation circuitry is unlikely.
questions.explanation: Addictive drugs differ, but many converge on mesolimbic dopamine activity. The shared pathway explains why diverse drugs can train pursuit.

questions.prompt: A treatment note says a client's drug feels duller now, so relapse risk should be low. Which response is best?
choices: Lower liking can sit beside cue-driven wanting, so risk may remain.
Lower pleasure means the drug has lost its motivational role in treatment.
Duller effects show the client mainly needs a higher dose to feel stable.
questions.explanation: Tolerance can reduce pleasure without removing sensitized wanting. A duller high can still leave cues with strong pull.

questions.prompt: A formulary team compares two forms with the same target: one hits fast, one arrives slowly. Which detail changes addiction risk?
choices: The total chemical target matters, while timing is mostly a side issue.
The fast form teaches more strongly by tying action to surge.
The slow form creates the same learning when the destination is shared.
questions.explanation: Fast onset strengthens learning because the act and chemical surge are close in time. Dose alone does not capture that risk.

questions.prompt: During intake at a recovery clinic, a counselor hears, "Craving only begins once someone has used again." Which case would challenge that claim?
choices: A person feels regret after using and then decides to seek help.
A person feels calm until withdrawal symptoms begin the next morning.
A person sees an old cue and starts seeking relief before using.
questions.explanation: Drug cues can activate prediction and pursuit before use. Craving can help cause relapse rather than merely follow it.

questions.prompt: A court program assumes a person will stop as soon as the costs are explained clearly. Which treatment plan fits addiction better?
choices: Treatment must address cues, stress, habits, and control, not only preference.
The costs should end use once they are made clear and concrete.
Intoxication preference explains enough if the person knows the risks.
questions.explanation: Obvious costs do not disable sensitized pursuit circuits. Treatment has to work with cues, stress, habits, and control together.

reviewCards.front: What does pathological wanting mean in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It means the pursuit system has learned to chase cues and promised relief even when the person no longer likes the result very much.

reviewCards.front: How can wanting grow while liking shrinks?
reviewCards.back: Dopamine can keep incentive pull high while pleasure systems give less reward. The person may report a weaker high and still feel a strong urge.

reviewCards.front: Why did the Olds and Milner rats matter for addiction thinking?
reviewCards.back: They showed that direct reward-circuit stimulation could make an animal work to repeat an action without food, water, or another ordinary prize.

reviewCards.front: What does anticipatory wanting (Ch 1) get wrong if you applied it naively to drug craving?
reviewCards.back: It can make the cue sound like normal future pull. In addiction, drug cues may be sensitized and relief-bound, so they can drive relapse before any drug appears.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of the addiction loop named here?
reviewCards.back: The loop is surge, cue learning, sensitized wanting, control erosion, and relapse risk. Each part helps explain why use can keep returning.

reviewCards.front: Why can relapse risk remain after withdrawal has passed?
reviewCards.back: Learned cues can keep incentive pull alive. A place, route, mood, or message can restart pursuit even when the body is no longer in acute withdrawal.

implementationPlan.title: Cut the Cue Chain
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice spotting the cue before you debate the craving. Cut the Cue Chain by removing one link that predicts relief: a route, contact, stash spot, payment path, or empty stretch of time. The aim is not perfect willpower. It is a few more seconds for control to return.

ifThenPlans.context: If an old cue appears before any use
ifThenPlans.plan: If an old cue appears, then Cut the Cue Chain by changing the next physical step before you decide what it means.

ifThenPlans.context: If the urge says the high will be worth it
ifThenPlans.plan: If the urge promises value, then Cut the Cue Chain by naming the last time liking failed to match the chase.

ifThenPlans.context: If a fast route makes use easy
ifThenPlans.plan: If the route is fast, then Cut the Cue Chain by adding one delay between action and effect.

ifThenPlans.context: If costs are obvious but the pull remains
ifThenPlans.plan: If costs are obvious and the pull remains, then Cut the Cue Chain by asking which cue, stress, habit, or control gap is active.

implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, explain Cut the Cue Chain to one other person in your own words. Use one cue, one relief promise, and one removed link as the example.

chapters.title: Domination
chapters.hook: You hover over Send, ready to win the argument, while the person on the other side becomes a target.
chapters.counterintuition: Control dopamine is not the enemy, but it turns dangerous when the next win makes people and facts look disposable.
chapters.tryThisNow: For about ten minutes during your next conversation about a win you want, write one honest cost line and read it aloud before you press.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Ambition builds when goals still answer to people, rules, and facts; domination begins when control dopamine tries to bend those checks into tools for the next win.

breakdown.fastRead: Rachel is halfway through the United States Anti-Doping Agency file when a lawyer asks her to soften the first page. The Lance Armstrong case is already big enough. It holds seven Tour de France titles, 2012 USADA sanctions, and a sport built around victory. Rachel stops sorting facts by trophy. She restarts by cost: who was pressured, who had to lie, what truth got buried. A win can become a leash. Control dopamine helps you chase a future prize; domination starts when the prize makes people and rules look like supplies.
breakdown.deepRead:
Nancy hears the Enron growth story in Houston while the present keeps interrupting. The public story says the future is bright. The hidden debt says the cash is not there. That is the grip of control dopamine: the brain's future tool can work for a promise before the present gives proof. In a healthy project, that helps you train, study, save, or build. You do work today for a better later. In domination, later starts bullying now. Jeffrey Skilling's Enron made projected value look present, while Andrew Fastow's hidden debt helped keep the picture clean until the 2001 bankruptcy forced reality back into the room. Paper success cannot pay real bills.

Winner effects add pressure. A prior win can make the next contest feel more reachable, so the appetite for one more win grows. That is not evil by itself. It is how athletes practice and founders survive boring days. The test comes when feedback hurts. If a teammate, rule, lab result, ledger, or tired body says stop, ambition can still listen. Domination tries to control the warning instead. In your life this can look smaller than Enron: you keep pushing a clever plan after the overdraft notice arrives, or you win an argument and forget the person has gone silent. The same circuit that plans the future needs present facts to keep it honest.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hailey reads a survey item aloud in the lab, and Bryce hears how polite hierarchy can sound. Felicia Pratto and Jim Sidanius gave this comfort with rank a name: social dominance orientation. It means a person is more at ease when groups are stacked, with some above and some below. The finding matters because domination is not always a fist on a table. Sometimes it is a calm survey answer that blesses a ladder.

That is why the warning is not a scold against ambition. Control dopamine is the part of wanting that lets you plan past the reach of your hand. It helps a rider train when the road hurts. It helps an executive build a company before the cash is there. It helps you finish a hard task when the present moment is dull. The danger arrives when the same future picture stops taking correction. Strategy needs a handrail of reality.

You can spot domination drift by walking through five parts: future prize, abstraction, control tactic, human cost, rationalized win. First comes the prize, like a title, a stock price, a rank, or the clean feeling of being right. Then abstraction pulls the prize away from bodies and bills. A tactic follows: hide the debt, pressure the witness, bend the rule, silence the person who slows the story. The cost lands in the present. The win then gets explained as necessary because the next prize will make it all worth it.

Lance Armstrong and Enron show different costumes for the same drift. Armstrong's titles made victory look like proof of a heroic self, until the 2012 USADA case pulled the control system into public view. Enron's Houston success story made the future look rich on paper, until hidden debt and the 2001 bankruptcy exposed the gap between story and cash. Neither case says every winner is corrupt. It says a win can start asking for protection.

The personal version is quieter. You promise yourself you care about honesty, then a message arrives that could make you look weak. You promise you care about your team, then a deadline makes a tired person look like a delay. You promise you care about home, then you chase one more advantage while the day fills with half-done tasks and the people near you get the leftover version of you. Control is not domination until it starts editing out the present.

Use the Cost Line when your goal starts making a person, fact, or rule feel like clutter. Say the prize plainly. Name the present cost plainly. If both sentences can stand in the same room, you may be looking at ambition. If the cost has to be hidden, renamed, or pushed onto someone with less power, the future has begun to eat the present.

Do the opposite when someone faces immediate harm or a clear duty is already yours. Do not pause to admire the machinery of motive when a child steps into traffic, a patient needs care, or fraud is in front of you. In those moments, act on the present fact first. The Cost Line is for seductive wins, not obvious emergencies.

examples.title: USADA Page Restart
examples.scenario: "Keep the team out of it," the rider says, and Rachel's practiced questions stop in the USADA interview. She had planned to move through Lance Armstrong's seven Tour de France titles one win at a time. The voice on the call makes the cost harder to miss. She has promised the record will not flatter winners, so she restarts with pressure, concealment, and the 2012 case that named the system.
examples.whatToDo: Rachel lets the silence change the order. She reads her promise aloud, then asks what the win required from people who had less power than Armstrong.
examples.whyItMatters: The restart keeps victory from setting the order of truth. When a prize asks for soft language, the pause gives present facts a vote.

examples.title: Houston Lobby Split
examples.scenario: The bright story is still smooth; the hallway outside Enron's Houston offices is not. Finance analyst Nancy stands with her badge in her hand as Enron's hidden debt starts becoming public. Jeffrey Skilling's growth case still travels through the hall, while people ask where the cash is. No speech is needed. Before the 2001 bankruptcy has a name in the room, the contrast teaches: a future number can sound cleaner than the bill in front of you.
examples.whatToDo: Nancy keeps the two claims together: the future value being praised and the cash question no one wants in the same sentence. She does not let the bright story stand alone.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene trains one habit you can use anywhere: hold the present cost near the future promise. Hidden debt wins when the promise gets the room to itself.

examples.title: Scale Item Exchange
examples.scenario: The senior coder is called away in the survey lab, and Hailey, a student analyst hired to tally responses, gets the table and the pencil. Bryce points to the item. "It says some groups should stay on top." "So this is anger?" he asks. "No," Hailey says. "Felicia Pratto and Jim Sidanius called it social dominance orientation. A calm answer can still bless a ladder."
examples.whatToDo: Hailey keeps the wording plain and speaks the hierarchy inside the answer. She refuses to let soft tone hide what the scale is measuring.
examples.whyItMatters: Domination is easier to miss when it sounds orderly. Naming the ladder helps you hear control before it turns into policy.

examples.title: Elevator Sentence Stop
examples.scenario: The elevator doors slide open onto a Houston hallway while Brandon is still explaining Enron's model to an analyst. He hears himself say Jeffrey Skilling's future value will cover the gap, then catches the words he skipped: Andrew Fastow's hidden debt. His own sentence is the error. Before the 2001 bankruptcy can be softened into background, he stops and names the cash hole.
examples.whatToDo: Brandon names the skipped words instead of improving the pitch. He says the debt line out loud and asks which present fact his own explanation tried to outrun.
examples.whyItMatters: Recovery starts at the moment you hear your own excuse. Catching it early keeps strategy from becoming a machine for ignoring facts.

examples.title: Stuck Memo Line
examples.scenario: The cracked phone screen catches Janet's thumb in her dining nook after Enron's 2001 bankruptcy. Analyst Janet is writing to a brother still drawn to the pitch. First line: "Do not count Jeffrey Skilling's promised future as cash." Next line: "Hidden debt is not a timing issue." The note closes with the cost of letting the story outrun the bill.
examples.whatToDo: Janet writes the boundary before she adds comfort. The saved draft makes the present fact plain enough that family loyalty cannot blur it.
examples.whyItMatters: A written line can hold still when pressure gets personal. If you cannot write the cost plainly, the win may already be editing the truth.

examples.title: Cold Coffee Forecast
examples.scenario: The coffee has gone cold in Presley's cup during a Houston forecast call about Enron. Review lead Presley starts with cash received, and the talk slows. Andrew Fastow's hidden-debt path keeps the cleaner number in view, and the talk stays smooth. Presley's claim shrinks to what can be checked. Fastow's path helps the 2001 bankruptcy arrive with the missing debt still loud.
examples.whatToDo: Presley ties the forecast to money already in hand. Fastow's path protects the clean story. The contrast shows ambition under constraint and control without it.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast gives you a test you can use fast. A goal is healthier when it survives contact with the bill, the body, or the rule.

questions.prompt: Rachel hears a reader say cheating winners belong in a separate ethics account, not in a dopamine account. Which reply fits the dopamine frame?
choices: Cheating winners fit because success-seeking can stretch into control and concealment.
Cheating winners belong elsewhere because dopamine explains desire, not rule breaking.
Cheating winners mainly show that pleasure matters more than future resources.
questions.explanation: The source frames winners cheating as one dopamine-linked puzzle. The near miss pushes cheating outside desire, but the dopamine frame treats domination as success-seeking extended too far.

questions.prompt: A case note says Lance Armstrong lost recognition for seven Tour de France titles after the 2012 USADA case. What does that detail show?
choices: The case was a brief lapse that mattered because one public title was at stake.
The case links repeated victory with concealment and pressure around the win.
The case is mainly about how fans misread ordinary training as wrongdoing.
questions.explanation: The sanctions covered a broad pattern, not one isolated mistake. Seven titles and the 2012 USADA case make the repeated win-at-cost pattern concrete.

questions.prompt: A log from Enron shows reported future value rising while hidden debt stays out of view before the 2001 bankruptcy. Which reading best fits?
choices: The company was mostly caught by a normal swing in energy prices.
The company had sound cash but suffered from weak public messaging.
The company let paper value displace present financial reality.
questions.explanation: The Enron fact centers hidden debt and accounting abuse. Energy prices or messaging are tempting side stories, but the key mechanism is future value replacing reality.

questions.prompt: Hailey sees a survey answer that calmly favors some groups staying above others. What should she recognize about social dominance orientation?
choices: It captures a short burst of anger that will fade when the room gets calmer.
It records a private wish to win one argument without touching group rank.
It measures comfort with hierarchy and unequal relations among groups.
questions.explanation: SDO is not just a hot mood or a single argument style. It measures a steadier preference for hierarchy and inequality between groups.

questions.prompt: A competition log shows Bryce becomes more eager after a streak of wins and more hesitant after repeated losses. What does that pattern suggest?
choices: Every new contest begins from zero once the last result is recorded.
Only fixed skill matters because prior outcomes cannot alter later drive.
Past wins and losses can change later confidence and competitive behavior.
questions.explanation: Winner and loser effects say prior outcomes can shape later engagement. The zero-reset reading misses how past contests alter perceived resource strength.

questions.prompt: Brandon keeps training for a future race even when today's workout feels dull and unpleasant. Which explanation fits control dopamine?
choices: Future rewards can energize present work even when the work feels bad.
Current pleasure must be high before motivation can keep a person moving.
Social approval is the only force that can carry effort through discomfort.
questions.explanation: Control dopamine can support planning without immediate pleasure. The tempting error is to assume motivation must come from enjoying the current task.

questions.prompt: During a planning call, Janet notices the forecast now describes two coworkers as barriers to a future deal. What is the danger signal in that wording?
choices: Any strategic plan is already abusive because it looks beyond the present.
People are being treated as instruments while present feedback gets discounted.
The deal is unsafe only if Janet stops wanting future success altogether.
questions.explanation: The risk is not strategy itself. Domination starts when people become tools for later outcomes and immediate human feedback stops binding the plan.

questions.prompt: Presley wants the promotion badly, but she still keeps the rule, the bill, and the tired teammate in view. How should she classify that drive?
choices: It is domination because any intense drive for success has the same moral shape.
It is ambition because the goal still works inside constraints that count.
It is passivity because caring about people means stepping back from the goal.
questions.explanation: The hard edge separates ambition from domination. Strong drive can stay healthy when rules, facts, and people still constrain the pursuit.

questions.prompt: A scandal file shows incentives, accomplices, and years of silence around a public champion. Which conclusion should Nancy draw?
choices: High-status misconduct often grows through systems that protect the reward.
High-status misconduct usually comes from one private impulse in one bad hour.
High-status misconduct mainly proves that public attention creates false blame.
questions.explanation: The source points to organized patterns over time, as in Armstrong and Enron. One bad moment is the shortcut the evidence pushes against.

reviewCards.front: How does control dopamine differ from domination?
reviewCards.back: Control dopamine plans for a future prize. It becomes domination when the plan starts treating people, rules, and facts as tools to bend instead of signals to respect.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of domination drift?
reviewCards.back: Domination drift moves through future prize, abstraction, control tactic, human cost, and rationalized win. The order shows how a goal can outrun reality step by step.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Lance Armstrong case show more than one bad rule mistake?
reviewCards.back: The 2012 USADA case cost Lance Armstrong recognition for seven Tour de France titles. That scale points to repeated concealment around victory, not one stray lapse.

reviewCards.front: What does social dominance orientation measure?
reviewCards.back: It measures comfort with hierarchy and unequal group relations. The key is not a passing aggressive mood; it is a steadier tilt toward ranked groups.

reviewCards.front: Recall anticipatory wanting (Ch 1): where does it bite in Rachel's Armstrong file?
reviewCards.back: It bites when Rachel sees the Armstrong file pulling attention toward future victory and status. Wanting the next win can outgrow liking the real cost of that win.

implementationPlan.title: Write the Cost Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching the moment a future prize starts shrinking the present. Write the Cost Line by putting the prize in plain words, then writing the present cost beside it. If the cost must be hidden, renamed, or pushed onto someone weaker, the plan is drifting toward domination.

ifThenPlans.context: When a goal makes a rule feel optional
ifThenPlans.plan: If the rule starts to feel like clutter, then Write the Cost Line: put the prize and the rule in one sentence, and keep both visible before acting.

ifThenPlans.context: When a spreadsheet makes people or cash disappear
ifThenPlans.plan: If the model looks clean but the bill is missing, then Write the Cost Line by placing the present debt beside the future value.

ifThenPlans.context: When rank starts sounding natural
ifThenPlans.plan: If hierarchy sounds calm and obvious, then Write the Cost Line by naming who gains power and who loses voice.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow ends, during your next conversation about a goal, write one line that names the present cost. Read it aloud and ask whether the win still deserves that price.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Write the Cost Line three times this week with widening difficulty: first on a private goal, next on a money or work choice, and last in a live disagreement.

chapters.title: Creativity and Madness
chapters.hook: 2 of the 4 steps make the wild idea; the other 2 keep it from becoming a private trap.
chapters.counterintuition: One open gate can feed art and break trust with reality: more signals can make a bright link, or make noise feel like proof.
chapters.tryThisNow: After your first drink of the day, pin a Signal Story Check note. Say, "A bright idea still needs a check," then log one cue.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a strange link flashes, Trace Before You Trust: loosened input and remote association need reality testing and crafted output before salience becomes work.

breakdown.fastRead:
Hazel wipes an equal sign from a seminar board: John Forbes Nash Jr., schizophrenia, 1994 Nobel. The mark was quick, but it carried the lazy story Hazel refuses. Salience is the brain's tag that says, pay attention; this matters. Dopamine helps place that tag. Importance is a feeling, not a verdict.

That matters when an idea flashes. The flash may be a useful link, or it may be noise wearing a crown. Creativity begins when you let the odd signal in, then ask what it can survive.
breakdown.deepRead:
A radiator click can become material instead of background. That is the small doorway into latent inhibition, the filter that helps you stop noticing familiar stuff that seemed useless before. When the filter weakens, the click, the color on the form, and a phrase in the hall may all reach awareness.

Shelley Carson, Jordan Peterson, and Daniel Higgins found a pattern in 2003: among people functioning well, a looser filter traveled with stronger creative achievement. Read the last part slowly. The finding is not a license to drown in every cue. It says extra input can help when the person still has enough control to sort it.

The creative control balance has 4 parts: loosened input, remote association, reality testing, and crafted output. The first 2 widen the field. The last 2 make the work shareable. A spark still needs a switch.

If you have ever caught a good idea from a stray sound, you know the gift. If you have ever lost an afternoon chasing a link that went nowhere, you know the cost. The useful skill is not to shut the gate. It is to write down the signal, name the story it suggests, and choose one check before you believe it.
breakdown.fullRead:
In a clinic note, D2 receptors do not look poetic. They look like part of a hard problem. The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia links positive symptoms to disturbed dopamine signaling, especially around D2 receptors. Positive symptoms include delusions and hallucinations. Antipsychotic antagonism matters here because many such drugs reduce D2-mediated signaling.

The model is useful, but it is not the whole disease. Schizophrenia is not simply too much dopamine everywhere. The source case gives you a narrower idea: a salience system can mark too much as meaningful. A street sign, a word on the radio, or a glance from a stranger can feel charged before reality has had a chance to answer.

You can feel a mild version of the problem when a coincidence grabs you. A friend mentions a city, then the same city appears in a headline. For a second, the world seems to be pointing. Usually you shrug and move on. In psychosis, the charge can arrive with force and conviction. The person is not choosing a quirky belief the way someone chooses a favorite song.

That difference keeps the caution humane. Curiosity loves a pattern, and art often begins with one. Illness can make the pattern feel personal, commanded, or impossible to doubt. When that happens, testing is not an insult to imagination. It is a guardrail for the person who is carrying too much meaning at once.

That is why Nash should not become a poster for the romance of madness. He received the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for game theory. He also began showing signs of mental illness in 1959 and lived through years of schizophrenia, treatment, and disruption. The prize does not erase the suffering. The suffering does not explain the prize.

A wide gate still needs a guard. In daily creative work, the guard is not cynicism. It is a plain check: can the idea be tested, shaped, and shown to someone else? A song line, a proof, a business idea, or a joke can start as a private jolt. It becomes creative when other minds can meet it without needing your exact mood.

The useful check is small. Write the cue that grabbed you. Write the story your mind made from it. Then choose one outside test: a source, a measurement, a trusted reader, or a version you can build. If the idea survives contact with the world, you can keep shaping it. If it collapses, you have saved time, money, and attention before the blown deadline becomes the lesson.

This advice misleads the friend who wants to treat a loved one's hallucination as hidden wisdom. Psychosis is not ordinary inspiration with better lighting. When a signal feels commanding, frightening, or impossible to test, the humane move is not to mine it for art. It is to protect the person first.

examples.title: Erased Equal Sign
examples.scenario: Hazel erases the equal sign while chalk dust is still floating above the seminar board. A student has linked John Forbes Nash Jr.'s schizophrenia to the 1994 Nobel as if one paid for the other. In the Princeton seminar room, the problem set lies open, and the learner's confusion is the lesson.
examples.whatToDo: Hazel rewrites the board as two true facts that do not cause each other. She keeps Nash's abstract achievement visible and names schizophrenia as a serious cost.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene protects admiration from turning into a myth. John Forbes Nash Jr. can be brilliant, receive the 1994 Nobel, and still not owe that brilliance to schizophrenia.

examples.title: Radiator Click
examples.scenario: Chantal is scoring a creativity packet in Shelley Carson's research office when the radiator click snaps her pen off the line. Last week the same sound faded under the task; now it pulls in the gray form, a hallway laugh, and a phrase she wants to test. The changed filter is the event.
examples.whatToDo: Chantal marks the extra cue, then writes one check beside it instead of following every branch. The packet still gets scored before the submission window closes.
examples.whyItMatters: Shelley Carson, Jordan Peterson, and Daniel Higgins found in 2003 that decreased latent inhibition can help high-functioning creators only when control keeps the flood usable.

examples.title: Clinic Wording
examples.scenario: There is barely enough time to fix the clinic note before copies go out, so psychiatrist Tobias reads one line to Cyrus in the clinic workroom: "Positive symptoms are dopamine." Cyrus taps the margin. "D2 receptors, especially. Not the whole illness." Tobias nods. "And antipsychotic antagonism is a clue, not the full map."
examples.whatToDo: Tobias changes the note from a sweeping claim to a narrower one. He ties positive symptoms to disturbed D2-related signaling and leaves room for the rest of schizophrenia.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps the dopamine hypothesis useful. D2 receptors and antipsychotic antagonism explain part of the pattern without making positive symptoms sound simple.

examples.title: Arrows Everywhere
examples.scenario: The draft is open at his desk after a late revision pass, and none of the arrows prove anything. Producer Cyrus thinks the blue receipt, the subway ad, and the unfinished chorus belong together. Maybe that is the gift. Maybe it is clutter. Lower latent inhibition does not mean every noticed thing is useful. One link first. One test next.
examples.whatToDo: Cyrus circles the link that can be checked and crosses out the rest for now. He lets the odd input stay, but he refuses to make the whole draft obey it.
examples.whyItMatters: Shelley Carson and Jordan Peterson's 2003 finding is easy to overread. The usable part is extra material plus control, not extra material alone.

examples.title: Pamphlet Space
examples.scenario: "So it is just dopamine," someone says inside the clinic printer station before the patient packet goes home, and trainer Lawrence stops dividing the pamphlet grid. The page has room for one short box on D2 receptors, one on positive symptoms, and one caution line about antipsychotic antagonism. The hard part is attention, not ink.
examples.whatToDo: Lawrence gives the D2 account a small, clear box and reserves space for the warning that schizophrenia is broader than one dopamine pathway.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning the page first prevents a partial model from becoming the whole story. Positive symptoms and D2 receptors matter, but the pamphlet must not flatten care.

examples.title: Two Bad Drafts
examples.scenario: "Keep the strange part," Asher says, and then the library carrel is Mathias's alone. Student Mathias weighs two bad drafts. One makes John Forbes Nash Jr.'s schizophrenia sound like the engine of the 1994 Nobel. The other cuts the illness until the life feels clean and false. Both protect him from saying the harder thing.
examples.whatToDo: Mathias chooses a third sentence. He writes that Nash's abstract power and schizophrenia coexisted, then names the illness as disruption rather than fuel.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma makes the caution practical. You can honor John Forbes Nash Jr. and the 1994 Nobel without making schizophrenia pay for genius.

questions.prompt: In Hazel's seminar, a student says Nash matters because of the movie. The bio lists John Forbes Nash Jr., game theory, and the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize. Which reading fits the record?
choices: It makes the later film the main source of his scientific standing.
It grounds his abstract achievement before the illness enters the case.
It treats public fame as better evidence than the economic prize.
questions.explanation: The Nobel fact anchors Nash's real work in game theory. The film story is not the evidence used here to establish his achievement.

questions.prompt: In the library carrel, Mathias wants to call Nash's illness a harmless eccentricity so the essay feels cleaner. Which reply best matches the timeline?
choices: The timeline supports that view because the illness stayed outside his life.
The timeline leaves the cost unclear because prizes erase impairment.
The timeline rejects that view because treatment and disruption marked later years.
questions.explanation: The source places signs of illness in 1959 and describes later treatment and disruption. Calling it a harmless quirk erases the cost.

questions.prompt: A lab note says decreased latent inhibition tracked higher creative achievement in high-functioning people. Which claim should survive?
choices: Lower filtering should improve creative work for any person in any state.
Lower filtering matters only when other mental skills are missing.
Lower filtering can help when other capacities keep extra input organized.
questions.explanation: The finding is narrow. It links lower filtering to creative achievement in high-functioning people, not to unbounded distraction for everyone.

questions.prompt: During packet scoring, Chantal keeps noticing a machine hum that used to disappear into the room. How should she read the change?
choices: She is screening out more familiar cues than before.
She is letting once-ignored cues enter awareness.
She is proving familiar cues have no creative use.
questions.explanation: Latent inhibition is reduced attention to familiar, once-irrelevant stimuli. A weaker filter lets more of those cues into awareness.

questions.prompt: Lawrence is writing one sentence about the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. Which version keeps the model accurate?
choices: It reduces schizophrenia to high dopamine across the whole brain.
It links positive symptoms to disturbed D2-related signaling while staying partial.
It replaces receptor talk with a purely social account of attention.
questions.explanation: The source ties positive symptoms to disturbed dopamine signaling, especially D2 systems. It does not make dopamine the whole disease.

questions.prompt: While revising the clinic note, Tobias says a delusion is just a belief someone chooses. Which response fits the salience frame?
choices: It agrees, since salience follows ordinary preference.
It agrees, since conviction alone creates the symptom.
It disagrees, since salience can charge a perception before testing.
questions.explanation: Psychosis is not ordinary preference. The salience frame says a perception or idea can feel important before the belief is tested.

questions.prompt: At his desk, Cyrus has a wild link between two ideas and a clean way to test it. Which sequence fits creative control balance?
choices: Let the link appear, then test whether it survives and can be shaped.
Keep the link private, since testing weakens the original spark.
Treat the link as finished, since surprise is the sign of value.
questions.explanation: Creative insight needs divergent association and convergent evaluation. Surprise starts the work; testing and craft make it usable.

questions.prompt: While revising his essay, Mathias writes in the margin, "This pattern feels important." Which inference fits dopamine and salience?
choices: The feeling marks a signal to inspect, not a fact already proved.
The feeling proves the pattern is accurate if it arrived suddenly.
The feeling should be dropped because charged patterns often waste time.
questions.explanation: Dopamine can help assign significance, but salience is not truth. A charged signal still needs a check.

questions.prompt: During Hazel's class discussion, a podcast clip claims madness is required for genius, and a student asks how to answer it. Which reply follows the source's caution?
choices: The overlap is limited, and illness should not be romanticized.
The overlap proves creators need psychotic symptoms to innovate.
The overlap means treatment risks removing creative capacity.
questions.explanation: The source allows a narrow overlap in mechanisms, then rejects the romance. Mental illness is not a source or requirement of creative achievement.

reviewCards.front: What does salience mean here, and why can it mislead?
reviewCards.back: Salience is the felt tag that says something matters. It can point you toward a useful clue, but the feeling of importance does not prove the signal is true.

reviewCards.front: How did Carson, Peterson, and Higgins connect lower latent inhibition to creativity?
reviewCards.back: In 2003, they reported that decreased latent inhibition was linked with higher creative achievement in high-functioning people. The key is extra input plus enough control.

reviewCards.front: What does the D2 dopamine hypothesis explain, and what does it not explain?
reviewCards.back: It links positive symptoms to disturbed dopamine signaling, especially around D2 receptors. It does not explain all of schizophrenia or reduce it to too much dopamine everywhere.

reviewCards.front: Why is John Forbes Nash Jr. a warning against the romantic genius story?
reviewCards.back: His 1994 Nobel honors game theory, while schizophrenia brought treatment, disruption, and years of struggle. The life shows coexistence, not illness as the price of genius.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more for a charged idea: wanting versus liking (Ch 1) or salience without enough filtering, and why?
reviewCards.back: Wanting versus liking explains chase and pleasure. With a charged idea, the sharper issue is salience: a cue can feel loaded before you know whether it is useful, true, or noise.

reviewCards.front: What are the four parts of creative control balance?
reviewCards.back: The four parts are loosened input, remote association, reality testing, and crafted output. The first two widen possibility; the last two make the work testable and shareable.

implementationPlan.title: Trace Before You Trust
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching the moment an idea feels bright before you believe it. Trace Before You Trust by logging the cue, the story it suggests, and one test. The move keeps loosened input useful without treating salience as truth.

ifThenPlans.context: If a pattern suddenly feels loaded with meaning.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the pattern feels loaded, then Trace Before You Trust. Write the cue, the story your mind added, and one way to inspect it.

ifThenPlans.context: If a new idea feels too exciting to edit.
ifThenPlans.plan: If excitement is pushing the draft forward, then Trace Before You Trust. Keep the link, but choose one reality test before adding more.

ifThenPlans.context: If extra cues keep pulling attention away from the main work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the cues multiply, then Trace Before You Trust on only one. Save the rest as raw material and return to the task.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone praises suffering as the source of your best work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise turns pain into proof, then Trace Before You Trust. Name the cost plainly and separate the work from the wound.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: The next time an idea feels unusually charged, say, "This feels important, so I will test it." Add one Signal Check row: cue, story, check.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, keep a daily Signal Check with three columns: cue that grabbed you, story it suggested, and check that changed or confirmed it. Circle one repeat cue at week's end.
